title: Spot the training myths
scenario: A teammate drafted an explainer for your team wiki: “How the assistant learns from us.” You need it to be accurate before it starts shaping how colleagues think about privacy and data use.
task: Select every claim that misstates how training and inference work. Leave the claims that are accurate.
response: Every message you send is used to retrain the model overnight. The model's weights are fixed once training finishes, so a conversation cannot change how it behaves for anyone else. I have updated my knowledge with everything you told me. The assistant will remember your preferences in future chats because we enabled the memory feature, which stores short notes and re-inserts them into new conversations. When you open a new chat, it starts with an empty context, so anything you want it to know must be re-supplied or stored.

claims.text: “Every message you send is used to retrain the model overnight”
claims.feedback: Automatic overnight retraining is a myth. Whether conversations are collected for future training at all is a decision written in the provider's policy — not a property of chatting.

claims.text: “The model's weights are fixed once training finishes, so a conversation cannot change how it behaves for anyone else”
claims.feedback: Accurate, and it is the core of the distinction: inference reads fixed weights.

claims.text: “I have updated my knowledge with everything you told me”
claims.feedback: Nothing was written into the model. At most, your text is still sitting in the context window — lose the chat and the “update” is gone.

claims.text: “The assistant will remember your preferences in future chats because we enabled the memory feature, which stores short notes and re-inserts them into new conversations”
claims.feedback: Correct framing: it is a stored note being retrieved, not a changed model — useful continuity with an editable, visible mechanism.

claims.text: “When you open a new chat, it starts with an empty context, so anything you want it to know must be re-supplied or stored”
claims.feedback: Exactly right, and it explains the everyday symptom: tomorrow's blank stare.

hints: Separate three layers: the weights (training), the conversation (context), and the product's notes store (memory).
Claims that attribute memory to the model itself — as if chatting wrote something in — are the ones to flag.
explanation: Two ideas do the work here. First, weights do not change during a conversation: inference reads them, it does not write them. Second, continuity comes from text being stored and re-supplied — context today or a memory note tomorrow. Any sentence that says the model itself learned from your chat crosses those layers; any sentence that keeps storage, context and weights separate is accurate.
